questions.topic: Counting semitones with a flat on the upper note
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a flat on the upper note does to a semitone count.
questions.stem: Bee yard note 3: Tobias wrote C4 to E4 as a major third of four semitones and then wrote C4 to E flat 4 as well; explain what the flat does to the count and to the name.

answer.exemplar: A flat lowers the upper note by one semitone, so the distance from C up to E flat is three semitones rather than four. The letter span stays a third because the note names are unchanged, and a third of three semitones is a minor third. The accidental therefore changes the size and the quality of the interval without changing its number, which is why both pairs are still thirds.

questions.explanation: Lowering the top note removes a semitone from the span, so four becomes three and the interval narrows from major to minor while remaining a third.
questions.hint: Ask what the count would be without the flat.

questions.topic: Counting semitones in a compound interval
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a compound interval relates to its simple form in semitone count.
questions.stem: Wax log 9: Halina asked why an interval above the octave is called compound; explain the idea and how the count is worked out.

answer.exemplar: An interval that spans more than an octave is called compound, and it is measured as its simple form plus an octave. A ninth is a second plus an octave, a twelfth is a fifth plus an octave, so the semitone count is the simple count plus twelve. A major ninth above C therefore holds fourteen semitones, because the major second inside it holds two of those semitones.

questions.explanation: A compound interval is its simple form plus an octave, so the semitone count is the simple count plus twelve, giving fourteen for a major ninth above C.
questions.hint: Reduce the interval to its simple form first.

questions.topic: Counting semitones in a major sixth
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a sixth major rather than minor.
questions.stem: Super log 15: Priya wanted to know why two sixths can sound quite different from one another; explain what fixes a sixth as major or minor.

answer.exemplar: The number of the interval is fixed by the letter names, so any span of six letter names is a sixth whatever the accidentals. The quality comes from the semitone count: a major sixth holds nine semitones, as from C up to A, while a minor sixth holds eight, as from C up to A flat. Because the same two letter names can be spelled with different accidentals, one sixth can be major and another minor.

questions.explanation: Both are sixths by letter span, and the semitone count decides the quality: nine for major and eight for minor.
questions.hint: Count the semitones once the letter names are fixed.

questions.topic: Counting semitones with a flat on the upper note
questions.learningObjective: State the rule for handling a flat on the upper note of an interval.
questions.stem: Nectar tally 27: Marisol wanted a rule for handling flats on the upper note; write the rule with a worked example in the logbook.

answer.exemplar: A flat lowers the note it sits on by one semitone, so on the upper note of an interval it pulls that note down and narrows the gap by one semitone. The letter names are untouched, so the interval number stays the same while the quality changes. For example C to E is a major third of four semitones, but C to E flat is a minor third of three semitones over exactly the same three letters.

questions.explanation: Because a flat lowers the upper note by one semitone, the span narrows by one and the quality changes while the interval number stays put.
questions.hint: Decide which direction the accidental moves the top note.

questions.stem: Swarm log 33: I need to explain in the logbook how the count of a compound interval relates to its simple form; write it out for the page.

answer.exemplar: Every compound interval can be reduced to a simple one by removing the octave, and the counting rule follows from that. The semitone count of the compound interval is the count of the simple interval plus twelve, so a tenth that contains a major third of four semitones contains sixteen. questions.explanation: The count of a compound interval is the count of its simple form plus twelve semitones for the octave.
questions.hint: Reduce the interval to its simple form and add an octave.

answer.exemplar: Look first at the letter names: if the span covers six of them then it is a sixth, whatever the accidentals have done. Then count the semitones. answer.exemplar: A flat is a lowering sign, so the note it marks sits one semitone below where the plain letter name would put it. On the upper note of an interval that means the top note comes down, the gap narrows by one semitone and the interval gets smaller while keeping its number. So C and E flat is a third of three semitones, a minor third, whereas C and E is a third of four semitones.

questions.topic: Counting semitones in a fifth reached with a sharp
questions.learningObjective: Count the semitones spanned by a fifth whose upper note carries a sharp.
questions.stem: Smoker record 52: tonight's question was the fifth from D4 up to A sharp 4, and the number of semitones must go into the log; what is it?
questions.explanation: D4 up to A4 is a perfect fifth of seven semitones, and the sharp on the upper note widens the span to eight, which is an augmented fifth.
questions.hint: Compare it with the perfect fifth a semitone lower.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in a compound interval with a flat
questions.learningObjective: Order compound intervals with a flattened upper note by semitone count.
questions.stem: Pollen log 53: four compound spans with a flattened upper note are C4 up to E flat 5, D4 up to G flat 5, C4 up to G flat 5 and C4 up to A flat 5; put them in order from smallest to largest.

options.text: D4 up to G flat 5, then C4 up to E flat 5, then C4 up to G flat 5, then C4 up to A flat 5
options.misconception: Swaps the compound tenth and the compound eleventh.

options.text: C4 up to E flat 5, then D4 up to G flat 5, then C4 up to G flat 5, then C4 up to A flat 5
C4 up to E flat 5, then C4 up to G flat 5, then D4 up to G flat 5, then C4 up to A flat 5
options.misconception: Puts the compound twelfth ahead of the compound eleventh.

options.text: C4 up to A flat 5, then C4 up to E flat 5, then D4 up to G flat 5, then C4 up to G flat 5
options.misconception: Reverses the order of the compound spans.

questions.explanation: The counts are fifteen, sixteen, eighteen and twenty semitones, so that is the running order. Each figure is the simple span plus the twelve semitones of the octave above it.
questions.hint: Count each span as its simple interval plus an octave.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in a minor seventh
questions.learningObjective: Compare the size of a minor seventh with a major sixth.
questions.stem: Swarm tally 54: I must explain in the log why a minor seventh sounds wider than a major sixth; which statement is true?

options.text: Both span the same ten semitones, so only the letter names tell them apart
options.misconception: Believes the semitone count says nothing at all.

options.text: The minor seventh spans nine semitones while the major sixth spans ten
options.misconception: Swaps the sizes of the seventh and the sixth.

options.text: The minor seventh spans ten semitones while the major sixth spans nine
The minor seventh spans eleven semitones while the major sixth spans nine
options.misconception: Adds a semitone to the minor seventh.

questions.explanation: The minor seventh holds ten semitones and the major sixth holds nine, so the seventh is the wider of the two by one semitone. That extra semitone is what makes the seventh sound more open.
questions.hint: Compare C up to B flat with C up to A.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in a major sixth
questions.learningObjective: Trace a semitone count for a major sixth.
questions.stem: Hive memo 55: my procedure for G4 up to E5 runs: name the letters G to E, a sixth; count the semitones of the minor sixth, eight; the upper note here is the natural E rather than E flat, so add one; report the total.

options.text: Seven semitones, because the letters G and E must be counted as a fifth
options.misconception: Reads the sixth as a fifth when counting.

options.text: Eight semitones, because the count of the minor sixth already fits this span
options.misconception: Leaves out the semitone that raises E flat to E.

options.text: Twelve semitones, because a sixth must be padded with an octave to be counted
options.misconception: Adds an octave to the simple sixth by mistake.

options.text: Nine semitones, because the natural upper note adds one to the eight of a minor sixth

questions.explanation: G4 up to E5 is a major sixth of nine semitones, one more than the eight of G4 up to E flat. The letter span settles the number and the count settles the quality.
questions.hint: Compare it with the span from G4 up to E flat.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting sharps in a key signature
questions.learningObjective: Identify the key that matches a stated key signature of sharps.
questions.stem: Drip record 56: my chart pairs four major keys with their sharps, and only one pairing is right; which row is it?

options.text: Row 2, which pairs A major with four sharps, adding the D sharp
options.misconception: Gives A major the signature of E major.

options.text: Row 1, which pairs A major with three sharps, F sharp, C sharp and G sharp
Row 3, which pairs E major with three sharps, F sharp, C sharp and G sharp
options.misconception: Gives E major the signature of A major.

options.text: Row 4, which pairs D major with three sharps, F sharp, C sharp and G sharp
options.misconception: Gives D major the signature of A major.

questions.explanation: Three sharps, F sharp, C sharp and G sharp, are the signature of A major and its relative minor, F sharp minor. The other rows shift the signature on to the neighbouring key.
questions.hint: Count the sharps in the fixed order from F sharp.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in a compound interval
questions.learningObjective: State how to tell a compound interval from a simple one.
questions.stem: Super note 57: Soren wants a short rule for telling a compound interval from a simple one; write it for the log page.

answer.exemplar: If the two note names are more than an octave apart, the interval is compound, and the quickest test is to count the semitones, since anything above twelve is compound. The name follows the letter span plus seven for the extra octave, so a span of a ninth is a second plus an octave and a span of a twelfth is a fifth plus an octave. For counting, take the simple interval and add twelve.

questions.explanation: Any span wider than an octave is compound, and its count is the simple interval plus twelve semitones.
questions.hint: Reduce the interval to its simple form to test it.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting the smallest interval in the system
questions.learningObjective: Count the semitones in the smallest step between two different pitches.
questions.stem: Brood entry 58: the exercise asks for the number of semitones from E flat 4 up to E natural 4, the smallest step between two different pitches; what number?
questions.explanation: E flat and E natural sit on neighbouring keys, so the step between them is one semitone, the smallest distance the system allows between two different pitches.
questions.hint: Think of adjacent keys on the keyboard.

questions.topic: Counting semitones with a flat on the upper note

questions.stem: Field tally 59: four spans with a flattened upper note are D4 up to F flat 4, G4 up to B flat 4, C4 up to F flat 4 and B flat 4 up to G flat 5; put them in order from smallest to largest.

options.text: D4 up to F flat 4, then C4 up to F flat 4, then G4 up to B flat 4, then B flat 4 up to G flat 5
options.misconception: Places the diminished fourth before the minor third.

options.text: G4 up to B flat 4, then D4 up to F flat 4, then C4 up to F flat 4, then B flat 4 up to G flat 5

options.misconception: Reverses the order of the four spans.

questions.explanation: The counts are two, three, four and eight semitones, so that is the running order. Each count is one semitone less than the same pair spelled with natural notes.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in a fifth reached with a sharp
questions.learningObjective: Describe a fifth whose two notes both carry a sharp.
questions.stem: Extractor log 60: the last drill of the season pairs F sharp 4 with C sharp 5; which statement describes that fifth correctly?

options.text: A major sixth of nine semitones, because the letters cover six names
options.misconception: Counts the letter span as a sixth by mistake.

options.text: An augmented fifth of eight semitones, because the sharps widen the interval
options.misconception: Widens the fifth even though both notes are raised together.

options.text: A diminished fifth of six semitones, because the sharp on the lower note narrows it
options.misconception: Applies the lower-note rule when both notes are sharped.

options.text: A perfect fifth of seven semitones, since both notes carry the same sharp

questions.explanation: Sharpening both notes of a fifth leaves the interval the same width, so F sharp up to C sharp is a perfect fifth of seven semitones. Sharpening only one of the notes is what changes the size.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when both notes move up together.
